hooks.text: The inevitable crash of our galaxy is actually a coin flip.
Is the Milky Way really doomed to collide with Andromeda?
Earth's certain destruction by a colliding galaxy was just a guess.

title: The 50/50 Chance of a Galactic Crash
description: A new study using data from Hubble and Gaia reveals that the Milky Way’s collision with Andromeda is far from certain.

beats.text: The inevitable crash of our galaxy is actually a coin flip.
beats.visual: Artist's concept of the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies colliding, NASA, 2012

beats.text: For over a century, astronomers warned the Milky Way would inevitably smash into the Andromeda Galaxy.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope wide field view of the Andromeda Galaxy, 2015

beats.text: Andromeda is currently hurtling toward us at one hundred and ten kilometers per second.
beats.visual: Illustration of the Milky Way galaxy seen from the outside

beats.text: A 2025 study led by Till Sawala used up to one hundred thousand simulations to test this fate.
beats.visual: Graphic of a galaxy evolution computer simulation

beats.text: It turns out the Large Magellanic Cloud acts like a cosmic bodyguard, pulling us off the impact course.
beats.visual: Hubble image of the Large Magellanic Cloud, 2013

beats.text: Data from the Hubble and Gaia telescopes now show only a fifty percent chance of merging.
beats.visual: Illustration of the Gaia spacecraft against a dense star field, ESA

beats.text: The chance of a head-on collision in five billion years is now estimated at just two percent.
beats.visual: Artist's concept of the night sky on Earth during a galaxy merger

beats.text: New calculations suggest the famous galactic crash is far from certain.
beats.visual: Distant view of two spiral galaxies passing each other closely
